The fragment for origin16 = p[0] << 16 overflows 64 bits when hi has bits in the top 16. Correct: fragment = (hi << 16) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF → i.e., only the low 48 bits of hi shifted up: fragment = (hi << 16) & MASK64. Since hi = frontkey<<48 | path bits, `hi << 16 & mask64` = (hi & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFF) << 16 ✓ = the address bits 16..63 at the high end of a 64-bit word. Yes: (hi & ((1<<48)-1)) << 16.

Similarly in the C++ builder: `inline_fragment` returns `p.hi << 16` for origin16 — in C++ with uint64_t, `<<` discards the overflow bits ✓ (defined behavior for unsigned) ✓ so it's fine there.

Let me fix pyref: frag = (p[0] << 16) & ((1<<64)-1) ✓.

Also, for origin16 with len ≤ 64: address bits 16..63 → the fragment holds bits [16,64) of the address at the top of the 48-bit field ✓.

Fix and re-run.

python3 -c "
import pyref, random
for seed in range(50):
    rng=random.Random(seed)
    n=rng.randint(1,60)
    pre=set()
    while len(pre)<n:
        hi=rng.getrandbits(64); lo=rng.getrandbits(64); l=rng.randint(0,128)
        hi,lo=pyref.norm(hi,lo,l)
        pre.add((hi,lo,l,rng.randint(0,4194302)))
    pre=sorted(pre)
    img=pyref.build_image(pre, rng)
    got=pyref.validate(img)
    assert got == {(p[0],p[1],p[2]):p[3] for p in pre}, (seed, len(got), len(pre))
print('pyref self consistent')
